title: The Barber's Tale of his Third Brother

keywords: the barber's tale of his third brother
full_text:
The barber then related the history of his third brother, Bakbak, who was blind from birth:

"My brother Bakbak was a blind beggar who walked the streets of Baghdad with a wooden staff, knocking on doors and asking for bread in the name of charity. One afternoon, he knocked upon the door of a large mansion. A voice from within cried: 'Enter!' Bakbak tapped his way into the courtyard and climbed the stairs, but when he asked for an alms, the owner said: 'I am as penniless as you, brother; I have nothing to give.' Bakbak replied: 'If you had nothing, why did you bid me climb all those stairs?' The master answered: 'Why did you knock upon my door?'

As Bakbak descended into the street, two wealthy thieves who had stolen a bag of ten thousand dinars were passing by. They noticed the blind man tapping his way into an abandoned bathhouse to rest. The thieves followed him in, thinking to hide their stolen treasure in the dry cistern. Bakbak, hearing their hushed whispers and the clinking of gold coins, realized that cutpurses were burying loot in the rubble.

When the thieves departed, Bakbak felt along the floor, unearthed the heavy bag, and concealed it inside his tattered cloak. But as he stepped into the sunlight, the thieves returned, seized him by the throat, and accused him of robbing their hoard. Though blind and helpless, Bakbak did not surrender to despair.

He cried out with a loud voice to the crowd in the street: 'Help, good citizens! These two ruffians have broken into the governor’s treasury and are trying to force a poor blind man to carry their stolen gold!' The captain of the city watch and twenty guards happened to be passing. Hearing the commotion, the guards rushed into the bathhouse, seized the two thieves, and recognized them as wanted brigands.

The magistrate rewarded Bakbak with one hundred dinars for his courage and returned the rest to the rightful merchants. My blind brother returned home with his head held high, proving that a clear mind and a fearless tongue can outmatch the sharpest eyes."
moral: Quick thinking and presence of mind can save a defenseless person from the cruelest cutpurses.
